title: The Data Center-Driven Drought is Coming for the West
author: Matt Sedlar
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/marblecanyon.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/07/the-
data-center-driven-drought-is-coming-for-the-west/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/glencanyondambw.jpg)

Glen Canyon Dam. Photo: Jeffrey St. Clair.

The federal government has [finalized a
plan](https://www.cnn.com/2026/07/31/climate/lake-mead-powell-colorado-water-
cuts-ca-az-nv) that will require California, Arizona, and Nevada to reduce
water usage from the Colorado River by 16 to 20 percent through 2028. But the
plan does not account for or even mention increased water usage caused by data
centers in both Upper and Lower Basin states. So is there a potential path
forward without tackling both?

The problem is a typical supply-and-demand issue. The Colorado River supports
40 million people, around 5.5 million acres of farmland, and vital ecological
habitats in seven states. This water is supplied by reservoirs along the
river, with the primary reservoirs being Lake Powell and Lake Mead. Both
provide 85 percent of storage for water usage in the basin, but both
reservoirs have fallen to historically low levels. As populations grow in
states like [Arizona](https://oeo.az.gov/news/arizonas-population-projected-
grow-more-two-million-2060), there isn’t enough fresh water to meet demand.

The US Bureau of Reclamation’s new plan focuses on Glen Canyon Dam and Hoover
Dam, which form Lake Powell and Lake Mead, respectively. Structural
complications for the dams will increase as water levels decline. The biggest
problem is that both dams are hydroelectric power plants, providing
electricity to the seven states. If the water level dips below a certain
level, it [renders the turbines inoperable](https://san.com/cc/what-does-low-
water-at-the-hoover-dam-mean-for-power-in-the-american-west/). Hoover Dam
alone generates enough power each year to serve [1.3 million
people](https://www.usbr.gov/lc/hooverdam/faqs/powerfaq.html) in the Lower
Basin. This means there is not enough electricity and water to meet demand,
and when you combine that with the basin states’ inability to come to some
sort of agreement, the Bureau of Reclamation is stepping in.

The latest changes are not for a lack of trying. In 2007, the Bureau of
Reclamation [initiated a
plan](https://www.usbr.gov/lc/region/programs/strategies/RecordofDecision.pdf)
that coordinated operational changes to Lakes Mead and Powell to minimize
future water shortages and avoid curtailments. These adjustments included
protocols for reservoir management during prolonged drought conditions,
alongside the development of Intentionally Created Surplus (ICS). This
mechanism encompasses various strategies, such as implementing high-efficiency
agricultural projects that result in excess supply, rigorous conservation
efforts, or introducing water from external sources into the reservoirs to
maintain critical surface elevations and prevent damage to dam infrastructure.
Despite all these changes, low reservoir conditions continue, and the 2007
agreement expires this year.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/marblecanyon.jpg)

The dwindling flow of the Colorado River through Marble Canyon, a few miles
below Glen Canyon Dam. Photo: Jeffrey St. Clair.

If that weren’t enough, the West is experiencing a boom in data center
construction. The irony is that California and Arizona are the [leading
states](https://www.datacentermap.com/usa/) in the Western US with high
concentrations of data centers, with Utah and Nevada trying to catch up. And
data centers rely on two things: water and electricity. The energy footprint
of data centers in Arizona now accounts for [7.4 percent of the state’s total
power](https://www.visualcapitalist.com/mapped-data-center-electricity-
consumption-by-state/), while in Phoenix alone, the water requirements for
nearly 60 of these facilities reach approximately [177 million
gallons](https://redcanarycollective.org/magazine/phoenix-data-center-water-
usage/#:~:text=Assuming%20that%2059%20of%20Maricopa,to%20cool%20data%20centers%20daily)
daily. And shockingly — or not, if you’re paying attention — Reclamation’s new
plan does not mention data centers. That’s because the administration has
[gone all in on AI](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-
content/uploads/2025/07/Americas-AI-Action-Plan.pdf), and that requires
building more data centers.

But don’t states, not the federal government, have control over where data
centers are built? Yes and no. Yes, city or county authorities control land
usage through regulations, zoning, and permitting, and states can take action
to curtail these efforts through environmental reviews, legislation, or
regulations. New York state, for example, just recently passed a
[moratorium](https://www.governor.ny.gov/news/first-statewide-moratorium-new-
hyperscale-data-centers-launched-governor-kathy-hochul) on new hyperscale data
centers by pausing state environmental permits.

But the federal government also plays a role in both interstate energy
management and environmental regulation. Trump has issued executive orders
[accelerating](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-
actions/2025/07/accelerating-federal-permitting-of-data-center-
infrastructure/) all federal permitting by bypassing environmental reviews. A
recent Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
[guidance](https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/epa-issues-permitting-guidance-
further-president-trumps-agenda-promoting-data-centers), for example, exempts
“islanded” power generation facilities — meaning they are not connected to the
public grid — from parts of the Clean Air Act, allowing developers more
flexibility in where they can build facilities. The administration has even
[offered federal land](https://www.energy.gov/articles/doe-
identifies-16-federal-sites-across-country-data-center-and-ai-infrastructure),
which bypasses all the state and local zoning issues. And as local opposition
has grown to the construction of data centers, the administration has directed
federal agencies to [review and potentially
withhold](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/12/eliminating-
state-law-obstruction-of-national-artificial-intelligence-policy/) federal
funding from states that pass overly restrictive AI or data center
infrastructure laws.

All of this brings us back to the Colorado River. Can any federal plan to
prevent water shortages in the Colorado River Basin work without
simultaneously banning data center development within the region? No. Using
less water can only get cities so far. Las Vegas actually has the strictest
and most progressive water policies in the country, with the Nature
Conservancy calling the city a “[water conservation rock
star.](https://adventure.com/how-las-vegas-conserves-water/)” And officials in
Arizona are attempting to restrict new housing developments based on
groundwater availability in the Phoenix area — even if efforts recently hit a
[roadblock](https://azmirror.com/briefs/judge-blocks-arizona-water-rule-that-
halted-new-housing-developments-across-the-valley/).

Localities can only do so much. And the frustrating part is that the federal
government has the power to work with state and local authorities to make
changes. Ideally, a plan would place a moratorium on the development of new
data centers in the basin while research examines current consumption levels.
If data centers’ water consumption exceeds a large percentage of the home
state’s allocation, new development should be permanently halted, and data
centers should be relocated or dismantled. This policy should include Upper
Basin states, like Colorado, New Mexico, and Wyoming, which have typically
been excluded from mandatory curtailments.

But when the administration has two policies that are at odds with each other,
the one that always wins out is the one that benefits corporate interests. And
right now, that’s AI — leaving the millions who rely on the Colorado River to
face the consequences.

_This first appeared on CEPR._
